book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with 'WPI measures the average change in wholesale prices', then lists the base year, the basket, the weights and the formula. Here inflation gets one line, then a household scene (this month's ration cost 5000; an elder says it used to cost 1000) builds the idea of comparing one basket at two times, and only then are 'basket' and 'base year' named, as labels for parts of the story. The supply chain (factory, wholesaler, shop, buyer) places WPI between PPI and CPI and gives a reason to care (a producer-side rise warns of consumer inflation) before the video narrows to WPI. The calculation is taught on one object, a chair, from 11 price quotes to its index, and that number is then joined by one line to its row in the weight table, so the big formula is built from a case the learner has already followed. How to read the result (100 in the base year, monthly, point-to-point) and who publishes it come last.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each piece answers the next question an index maker must settle, in the order they settle it: what to compare (basket), against when (base year), at which point of the chain (wholesale), which goods and how heavy (groups and weights), how to price one item (quotes to elementary index), how to combine items (weighted sum), and how to read the result (base 100, monthly, point-to-point).

opening.what: Says in plain words that prices of goods and services rising year after year is called inflation, and that the government measures it with two indices, WPI and CPI, expanded at once; the screen shows a grocery bag and a delivery rider beside empty price-vs-year axes.

moves.concept: inflation and the two indices WPI and CPI
moves.what: Inflation in common language: prices keep rising year after year.

moves.concept: inflation and the two indices WPI and CPI
moves.what: Government measures inflation with indices named WPI and CPI, which mean Wholesale Price Index and Consumer Price Index.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: These are technical terms, but the idea is in everyday home talk: you bring the month's ration, someone asks the cost, you say 5000, and an elder says in our time this much came for 1000.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: Observes the conversation as data: this basket cost 1000 in grandfather's time, 5000 today, 'yaani' a 400% rise.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: 'Chaliye' see how this idea is related to WPI and CPI.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: Governments first list the commodities households commonly use; this standard set is called the basket.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: A reference point is needed to compare today's prices with, which in our story was grandfather's time; it is called the base year.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: Current base year 2011-12, a fiscal year, 'yaani' April 2011 to March 2012.

moves.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now
moves.what: A survey finds today's prices of the basket's goods, and comparing them with base-year prices shows how much they rose.

moves.concept: supply chain price points: producer, wholesale, consumer price and PPI, WPI, CPI
moves.what: Point to note: the basket differs for wholesale buying and for consumers like us.

moves.concept: supply chain price points: producer, wholesale, consumer price and PPI, WPI, CPI
moves.what: Factory sells to wholesale dealers, they sell to retail shops, shops sell to consumers; at each step a different price: producer price, wholesale price, retail or consumer price.

moves.concept: supply chain price points: producer, wholesale, consumer price and PPI, WPI, CPI
moves.what: The indices that measure the average level of these three prices: PPI 'yaani' producer price index, WPI, CPI.

moves.concept: why a producer-side index warns early: a price rise travels down the chain
moves.what: 'Maan lijiye' the producer sells to the wholesaler at 10; the wholesaler sells to retailers at 15, adding profit and costs such as transport; the retailer adds a margin again.

moves.concept: why a producer-side index warns early: a price rise travels down the chain
moves.what: If the producer raises prices for some reason, wholesale prices will surely rise and in the end consumer prices too.

moves.concept: why a producer-side index warns early: a price rise travels down the chain
moves.what: So by watching PPI the government learns before inflation rises, because goods take time to reach consumers, and fiscal and monetary policy can act early.

moves.concept: WPI scope: first point of bulk sale, use in policy
moves.what: But India measures inflation with WPI and CPI, not PPI; the effort is to bring WPI as close to PPI as possible.

moves.concept: WPI scope: first point of bulk sale, use in policy
moves.what: WPI takes only prices at the first point of bulk sale in the domestic market, 'yaani' when the wholesaler first sells to retailers.

moves.concept: WPI scope: first point of bulk sale, use in policy
moves.what: WPI is used for macro-level policy making, whereas CPI is used for micro-level (claim given without a reason; doubtful as stated).

moves.concept: WPI scope: first point of bulk sale, use in policy
moves.what: Today's video focuses on WPI (CPI next).

moves.concept: WPI basket: 697 commodities in three groups with weights
moves.what: The wholesale basket has 697 commodities in three parts: fuel and power, manufactured products, primary articles, each with its sub-groups and examples.

moves.concept: food articles vs non-food articles vs food products
moves.what: Voices the learner's confusion: primary articles has food articles, and manufactured products also has food products, so what is the difference? Answered by examples.

moves.concept: food articles vs non-food articles vs food products
moves.what: Food articles grow naturally and can be eaten (cereals, pulses, milk); non-food articles grow naturally but cannot be eaten (raw cotton, jute, silk); food products are processed (sugar, tea, chocolate, noodles).

moves.concept: WPI basket: 697 commodities in three groups with weights
moves.what: So wholesale commodities are divided into three parts.

moves.concept: WPI basket: 697 commodities in three groups with weights
moves.what: Their weights differ: manufactured products highest at 64.23%, primary articles 22.62%, fuel and power lowest at 13.15%.

moves.concept: WPI basket: 697 commodities in three groups with weights
moves.what: Further break-up into items with individual weights; only food products (9.122%) is read out, and adding all items gives 64.23%.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: 'Chaliye' see how WPI is actually calculated, with the example of furniture: a chair.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: A chair sells at different prices in different places, so many quotations are collected for each item (8331 in all); more quotations, more accurate WPI.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: 'Maan ke chalte hain' 11 quotations for this chair, each with a base price ('yaani' its 2011-12 price) and a current price.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: Indirect taxes (GST) are left out of both prices, because WPI should not move with fiscal policy.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: Price relative = current price divided by base price, times 100, for each quotation.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: The geometric mean of all the price relatives is the item's elementary price index.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: Earlier this was an arithmetic mean; why switch to the geometric mean? Write in the comments. Never answered in the video.

moves.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)
moves.what: This two-step calculation (price relative, then geometric mean) is the Jevons index formula; we now have the chair's index, called I1.

moves.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)
moves.what: The chair's weight in the table is W1; do this for every item, multiply each index by its weight, add them all and divide by the total weight.

moves.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)
moves.what: The total weight is obviously 100; this formula is the Laspeyres index formula (name garbled by recognition).

moves.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)
moves.what: 'Yaad kijiye': the I inside the Laspeyres formula was found with the Jevons formula: one formula nested in the other.

moves.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)
moves.what: So we understood how WPI is calculated; it is done every month.

moves.concept: base year reads 100 in every month
moves.what: For the base year every month's WPI is 100: check it without pen and paper: current price = base price gives price relative 100, every item's I is 100, it cancels top and bottom, the answer is 100. 'Just know why we say what we say.'

narration.density: About 35 terms (inflation, index, WPI, CPI, basket, base year, fiscal year, producer, wholesale and consumer price, PPI, first point of bulk sale, macro and micro policy, commodities, fuel and power, manufactured products, primary articles, food articles, non-food articles, minerals, food products, weight, quotations, base price, current price, indirect taxes, GST, price relative, arithmetic and geometric mean, elementary price index, Jevons, Laspeyres, point-to-point, DPIIT, DIPP) in about 840 s, about 2.5 per minute. talmel_summary: Picture and voice mostly land together or with the picture a second or two ahead; the one voice-first tile is the 400% table. The fit is best where the picture is the thing being explained: the story beats drawn as bubbles and then turned into a basket/then/now table, the supply chain with a coloured band on each sale, the chair's table growing column by column with a bracket gathering the price relatives, the August column boxed against base August, and a cable from the ministry to a megaphone for 'publishes'. Weak: labels that only write the term (index names, India badge, macro chip), a 44 s dense weight table of which one value is spoken, and on-screen numbers never spoken (20 Rs, 193.77, the 2022-23 values). The transcript is nearly complete (one 6 s gap at 466-472 s), but recognition garbles the Laspeyres and Jevons names.

voice.notes: About 178 words per minute, calm and explanatory, many 'basically', 'yaani', 'maan lijiye', 'chaliye'. Percentages read with 'point' (64.23, 13.15); the formula read aloud in words (current price ko base price se divide, multiply hundred). Stress words: 'bahut hi important point, kisi bhi haal mein miss nahi karna chahiye' before point-to-point. One direct question to the viewer with a comment-box prompt. Formula names (Laspeyres, Jevons) pronounced so that recognition hears them as Hindi words; BIE's voice needs a pronunciation entry for such names.

game_ideas.player_does: Works as the index office for one item, a chair: taps cities on a map of India to collect price quotes (base and current), drops each quote into the table, then chooses how to combine the price relatives (arithmetic or geometric mean).
game_ideas.process_happens: Each quote becomes a price relative (current / base x 100) in the column; the chosen mean produces the chair's elementary index; one outlier quote (a cheap base price that tripled) visibly drags the arithmetic mean up more than the geometric mean; the index then slides into the chair's row and is multiplied by its weight.
game_ideas.win: A correct elementary index from enough quotes, placed into the weighted total.
game_ideas.lose: Adding GST to a price shows the index jumping with a tax change ('fiscal policy moved WPI'); too few quotes shows a wide error band; the arithmetic mean shows the outlier's pull (answering the video's unanswered question).
game_ideas.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)

game_ideas.player_does: Acts as policy maker watching three meters (PPI, WPI, CPI) on the supply chain; a random shock raises a producer's price, and the player decides when to pull a policy lever.
game_ideas.process_happens: The price pulse travels with a delay: producer band, then wholesale band, then consumer band; prices 10, 15, 20 tick up in turn; the lever slows the pulse only if pulled early.
game_ideas.win: Act on the PPI or WPI signal so CPI stays under the line.
game_ideas.lose: Waiting for CPI to move shows the rise already reaching shoppers; acting on no signal shows a needless slowdown.
game_ideas.concept: why a producer-side index warns early: a price rise travels down the chain

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts goods into the WPI basket groups: wheat, milk, raw cotton, jute, coal, electricity, sugar, noodles, chocolate, minerals.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each item drops into fuel and power, primary articles (food, non-food, minerals) or manufactured products (food products and others); a weight bar fills toward 13.15 / 22.62 / 64.23.
game_ideas.win: All items in the right group and sub-group.
game_ideas.lose: Putting sugar or noodles under food articles asks 'grown or processed?' and moves it to food products; putting raw cotton under food articles asks 'can it be eaten?'.
game_ideas.concept: food articles vs non-food articles vs food products

game_ideas.player_does: Sets the three group weights of a toy basket, then applies a 10% price shock to one group at a time.
game_ideas.process_happens: The index needle moves by weight x shock; a shock to manufactured products (heavy) moves it far more than one to fuel and power (light).
game_ideas.win: Predict which shock moves the index most before applying it, and get the real weights in the right order.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong guess shows the needle moving little or much with the weight-times-shock sum spelled out.
game_ideas.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)

game_ideas.player_does: Fills a basket at today's shop and at the base-year shop, then turns the two totals into an index.
game_ideas.process_happens: Totals appear (1000 then, 5000 now), the price-relative formula turns them into 500, and the rise reads 400%; changing the base year changes every number.
game_ideas.win: Correctly state both the index (500) and the % rise (400%) from the same two totals.
game_ideas.lose: Saying the index is 400 shows the gap between 'index' and 'rise', with 100 as the base marker.
game_ideas.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now

notes_questions.q: Inflation kya hai aur India mein ise measure karne ke liye kaun se index hain?
Basket aur base year kya hote hain? Dada ji ke 1000 aur aaj ke 5000 wali kahani se samjhaiye.
Producer, wholesale aur consumer price chain mein kahan lagte hain, aur PPI, WPI, CPI kis point ka price lete hain?
PPI par nazar rakhne se sarkar inflation ko pehle kaise pakad sakti hai?
WPI basket ke teen group aur unke weights kya hain?
Food articles, non-food articles aur food products mein kya farq hai? Do-do udaharan dijiye.
Ek item (chair) ka elementary price index kaise nikalta hai: quotations se price relative se geometric mean tak?
WPI mein indirect taxes (GST) kyon nahi jode jaate?
Arithmetic mean ki jagah geometric mean kyon? Ek mehenga outlier quote dono par kya asar dalta hai?
WPI ka formula kya hai, aur Jevons aur Laspeyres formula iske kis hisse mein lagte hain?
Base year ke har mahine ka WPI 100 kyon aata hai?
WPI data kaun publish karta hai, aur pehle uska naam kya tha?

checks_learned: A question put to the viewer (arithmetic vs geometric mean) must be answered later in the same video, or the script fails.
Every number shown on screen must be spoken or labelled as reference: here 20 Rs, the chair's 193.77 and the 2022-23 monthly values were shown but never said.

When a story sets numbers (1000 then, 5000 now) and a formula comes later (current / base x 100), the formula must be applied to the story's numbers once (index 500 vs rise 400%); here that link was missed.
A data table on screen shows only the rows the narration names; a 22-row weight table held for 44 s with one value spoken should be collapsed or stepped through.
Named formulas and proper nouns (Laspeyres, Jevons, DPIIT) need a pronunciation entry for BIE's voice and subtitles taken from the script, since recognition garbled them here.
A running example started on one item (the chair) must be carried into the aggregate step on screen (done here with one line from I1 to W1); enforce for every worked calculation.
Time-bound remarks ('we are in December 2022', months not yet available) must carry a date stamp or be removed.
Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: WPI for macro vs CPI for micro policy, and 'point-to-point' explained as comparison with the same month of the base year.

teaching_best.why: A household scene (5000 now, 1000 in an elder's time) builds the comparison first; 'basket' and 'base year' are then named as labels for parts of the story the learner already holds.
The supply chain with prices 10, 15, 20 and a what-if (the producer raises prices) gives a reason for indices at different points: a producer-side rise warns of consumer inflation.
The learner's likely confusion (food articles vs food products) is voiced and cleared with everyday examples: grown and edible, grown and not edible, processed.
One chair is followed through the whole calculation: quotes, price relatives, geometric mean, its index, its weight row, the weighted total.
Why the base year reads 100 is shown by reasoning, not stated: put current = base into the formula and everything cancels to 100.

teaching_weak.why: The 400% rise is never tied to the index value (500) the formula would give, so 'rise' and 'index' are left unconnected.
'WPI for macro, CPI for micro policy' is stated without a reason and is doubtful as stated.
A dense, real weight table sits for about 44 s with only one value spoken.
The arithmetic-vs-geometric mean question is sent to the comment box and never answered.

The point-to-point rule is stressed as a must-know, but the explanation (compare with the same month of the base year, because of seasonal items) is doubtful and the on-screen 2022-23 values are not read.
